title: Latency Dive: Profiling Playbook and CI collectors
body:
Purpose:
This playbook captures a repeatable procedure for investigating production or perf-ci regressions where the primary symptom is elevated request latency (p95/p99). It bundles the recommended automated collectors, local/offline scripts, and CI job definitions we use to gather minimal reproducible artifacts (profiles, traces, flamegraphs, minimal perf traces) that let an engineer triage root cause without long-running manual sessions.

Scope and assumptions:
- Targets serving-runtime worker processes (GPU and CPU paths), and the request path from HTTP front-door to model compute and back.
- Focused on latency (tail behavior). Throughput regressions are out of scope unless they correlate with increased latency.
- Assumes access to perf-enabled images in CI and a debug build of the runtime (symbols enabled).

Quick triage checklist (first 15–30 minutes):
1) Confirm metric delta: what changed (p50/p95/p99, error rate, backend queue length) and when.
2) Identify rollout or infra events: new model, quantization change, scheduler rollout, kernel upgrade, instance types, scaling/new region.
3) Reproduce locally with a narrow synthetic workload: single model, fixed prompt, controlled concurrency (see benchmarks/seq_bench.py).
4) Run automated collector (short capture) to get a first flamegraph and traces (see scripts/collect_latency_snapshot.sh).
5) Correlate with traces and logs (OpenTelemetry spans, request ids).

Automated CI perf job (recommended job: ci/perf-jobs/latency-snapshot.yml):
- Trigger: nightly, on merge to main, and optionally on model / runtime changes via labels. Also run manually from pipeline UI.
- Image: perf-enabled debug image (debug symbols, /usr/lib/debug mounted).
- Workload: 60s warmup + 120s capture at traffic shape matching customer load; two concurrency profiles: low-concurrency single-request p99, and steady 50qps steady-state.
- Artifacts: perf.data, folded-stacks.txt, flamegraph.svg, otel-export.json, system-metrics.csv. Kept for 30 days in ci-artifacts/perf/latency-snapshots/.
- Alerts: job fails if p95 increases above baseline or if flamegraph shows >40% time in new kernel/user function (heuristic).

Collector scripts (repo paths and brief descriptions):
- scripts/collect_latency_snapshot.sh — high-level orchestrator used by CI and on-call. Steps: start system metrics collector (node_exporter-lite), run load generator (benchmarks/seq_bench.py), run perf record -F 99 -g -a -o perf.data (or per-process if containerized), dump otel traces via otel-agent snapshot, stop collectors, run post-processing to produce flamegraph.svg.
- tools/parse_perf_to_folded.py — converts perf script output into folded stacks for flamegraph.pl.
- tools/gen_flame_from_perf.sh — perf script | tools/parse_perf_to_folded.py | FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl > flamegraph.svg
- scripts/collect_ebpf_latency.sh — lightweight eBPF collectors (bcc/bpftrace) to capture syscall & schedule latencies and kernel blocking stacks for p99 spikes.

Example perf commands (notes below about flags):
- Full-system sample (CI): sudo perf record -F 99 -g -- sleep 120 -o /tmp/perf.data
- Per-process (dev): sudo perf record -F 200 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 60 -o /tmp/perf.data
- Convert: sudo perf script -i /tmp/perf.data > /tmp/perf.out
- Fold: python3 tools/parse_perf_to_folded.py /tmp/perf.out > /tmp/folded.txt
- Flame: FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl /tmp/folded.txt > /tmp/flame.svg
Notes: use -F 99 or 199 adjusted for short captures; sampling too high causes overhead, too low misses hotspots.

eBPF traces and bpftrace one-liners (for kernel-side tail investigation):
- syscall duration heatmap: sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_* { @[probe] = count(); }' (tweak probes)
- scheduling latency probe (bpftrace): sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:sched:sched_switch { @[comm] = hist(nsecs); }' to see wake-to-run delays.
- bcc script: /tools/bcc/resolve_blocked_threads.py — finds tasks stuck in uninterruptible sleep often due to NVMe or driver waits.

Correlating profiles to distributed traces and logs:
1) Ensure request-id is injected into runtime logs and OTEL span attributes. 2) When perf capture is collected on a host, run a short tracer that exports spans (otel-export.json) containing timestamped trace ids; match the highest-latency request ids to CPU stacks around their timestamps. 3) Use the bench/generator to stamp a known header X-Debug-Req: <uuid> to make correlation trivial in noisy systems.

Interpreting flamegraphs (common patterns):
- Large wedge in user-space runtime scheduler paths -> look at batching or backpressure changes, or new locks.
- Time in kernel: scheduling or I/O (NVMe) — check driver/kernel versions and NVMe IO stats.
- Deep stacks in model library (cuBLAS/cuDNN) that expand during specific sequence lengths -> check dynamic kernel selection / compilation cache flushes.
- Repeated short spikes across many threads -> suspect lock convoy, memory allocator contention, or futex wait.

Practical debugging tips and knobs to test:
- Rebuild with jemalloc vs system malloc to check allocator hotspots.
- Disable dynamic frequency scaling and CPU turbo when doing apples-to-apples perf comparisons (BIOS or cpufreq governor).
- Pin worker threads to cores (taskset) to remove scheduler noise.
- Run with environment RWKV_BATCH=1 or similar to force different batching paths if investigating batching regressions.
- Test with CPU-only worker to split GPU driver noise from user code.
- Re-run CI collector on older commit (bisect) to find the commit that introduced the regression.

Retention and artifact governance:
- CI perf artifacts are stored for 30 days by default. If a job fails or an investigation begins, move artifacts to long-term archive s3://redwood-perf-archive/<investigation-id>/ and tag the issue key.
- Perf data may contain symbols; scrub secrets before sharing externally.

Playbook step-by-step (detailed):
1) Gather metrics and scope (observability dashboard screenshots, time window, commit hash, rollout id).
2) Kick off a controlled CI snapshot (ci/perf-jobs/latency-snapshot.yml) for the same commit/branch.
3) Run collect_latency_snapshot.sh locally in debug image with identical flags to CI for reproducibility.
4) Generate flamegraph.svg and otel-export.json; open both side-by-side and mark timestamps for top p99 requests.
5) If flamegraph shows user CPU hot path, instrument the function with micro-benchmarks and binary-search smaller changes (toggle flags).
6) If kernel or I/O is implicated, collect iostat, nvme-cli, and dmesg; escalate to infra if driver/kernel change is suspected.
7) If no smoking gun, run eBPF collector for a longer window (5–10 minutes) and follow up with a focused per-request sampling (attach to PID and use perf record -p <pid> --call-graph dwarf).
8) Document findings in the incident ticket (INF-xxxx), attach artifacts, and propose a fix/rollback.

Common pitfalls and anti-patterns:
- Taking too-short traces (5–10s) in systems with long-tail behaviors; capture at least 3–5x the known p99 latency.
- Comparing non-symbolized perf.data across builds — always use the debug symbol image or mount /usr/lib/debug.
- Running perf on heavily virtualized instances without kernel-perf support; prefer container runtime with --privileged for CI when allowed.
- Ignoring NUMA/placement differences — latency increases often correlate with wrong CPU/GPU affinity or unexpected cross-socket traffic.

Useful local dev commands and short-hands (copy-paste):
- ./scripts/collect_latency_snapshot.sh --duration 180 --concurrency 4 --outdir /tmp/invest123
- ./tools/gen_flame_from_perf.sh /tmp/invest123/perf.data /tmp/invest123/flame.svg
- python3 benchmarks/seq_bench.py --target http://localhost:8080/generate --qps 10 --duration 120 --headers 'X-Debug-Req:DEV-<id>'

Next steps and TODOs (owner: Aisha Patel):
- [ ] Add a lightweight Kubernetes DaemonSet collector that mounts debugfs and runs eBPF collectors without privileged pods (RFC in review).
- [ ] Add baseline flamegraphs per model variant to perf-dashboard to enable automated diffing.
- [ ] Improve ci/perf-jobs to run differential flamegraph comparison vs baseline and surface top-changes in GitHub PR comments.

Notes and references:
- Internal PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/422 (perf job templates)
- Confluence: CONFLUENCE-RT/latency-dashboards (dashboards + runbook links)
- Kernel/perf guide: https://perf.wiki.kernel.org/index.php/Main_Page
- Brendan Gregg FlameGraph: https://www.brendangregg.com/flamegraphs.html

Contact and escalation path:
- First responder (on-call): eng-serving-runtime on-call rotation -> Slack #eng-srv-runtime.
- Escalate to infra for suspected driver/kernel/hw faults.

Appendix A: Minimal reproducible workload (benchmarks/seq_bench.py excerpt):
- Sends fixed prompt with deterministic tokens at varied sequence lengths to trigger model code-paths that change compute kernels. Use --seed to ensure identical tokenization across runs.

Appendix B: Example naming conventions for artifacts:
- <investigation-id>_perf_<commit>_YYYYMMDD.perf.data
- <investigation-id>_flame_<commit>_YYYYMMDD.svg

If you use this playbook, add a short note to the investigation ticket summarizing which scripts you ran and link the artifact paths so future folks can reproduce the same snapshot.
